predictions.text: Directors Whose Earlier Work Makes You Look at Them in a Completely Different Light? My first exposure to the films of Jonathan Demme was THE SILENCE OF THE LAMBS and PHILADELPHIA. As such, I had thought of him as the maker of serious dramas. But a few months ago I finally watched Demme's SOMETHING WILD (1986), which I loved. What I didn't expect was how wacky both SOMETHING WILD and MARRIED TO THE MOB (1988) are and just how adept Demme seemed to be at directing comedy. Those two movies completely opened my eyes. Has anyone had a similar experience watching a different filmmaker's earlier output, where you had previously thought of them as strictly making movies of a particular sort, but subsequently realized they were more versatile than you had originally thought?

Trivia of the Week: Constance Miller was already in the shop when McCabe went to buy three girls for $200 in McCabe & Mrs. Miller (1971). Do you ever wonder how Constance Miller suddenly shows up and starts talking McCabe into letting her manage the whorehouse? Well, it's kind of a cool, blink-and-you'll-miss-it detail, but she's already inside the shop in Bearpaw (the next town) when McCabe goes to buy three girls for $200 from the pimp. You can spot Mrs. Miller just inside the doorway when the pimp briefly opens it to bring one of the whores out. McCabe doesn't meet her then, but she must've either learned about him from the pimp or overheard the pimp say, "You don't know what you're doing, McCabe. You got no experience at this." Even in that brief glimpse, you see her rubbing her nose. What does that tell you? She must be on something.

I'm not sure which True Grit I like better. I rewatched this for the first time since 2010. I also rewatched the original John Wayne movie before my rewatch. I think both movies are pretty great. I was surprised how many lines in the 2010 movie were ripped directly from the original. I think the casting and performances in the 2010 movie were very good, probably better than the original, overall. I do think that the original has better filming locations and a better color palette. I didn't like the change, in the remake, that has Maddie kill Chaney with the Sharps instead of her father's Colt. Both movies foreshadow the gun being too large for her to handle. When she kills Chaney with the Colt, the recoil makes her stumble into the pit. The new movie does have her stumble into the creek from the Colt recoil when she shoots Chaney the first time, but I felt that having it happen with the killing and the pit was more fitting. I did like that the new movie let LaBeouf live (apparently this is true to the book) instead of anti-climatically dying, like in the first movie.

[Contains Spoilers] Trains Dreams was a beautiful movie. Brilliant Acting. But I simply do not believe the narrator at the end. "But on that Spring day, as he misplaced all sense of up and down, he felt at last, connected to it all." Robert Grainier spent close to forty years of his life lonely, rudderless, and miserable. Am I really supposed to believe that it was all worth it because in the end he gets to take a 10 minute plane ride before he dies? I call bullshit. This was a man who desperately craved a scrap of goodness in his life. I think he imagined a sense of connection because he wanted it so badly that he was able to fool even himself for a moment. Here is a man who knew his life was complete shit and did almost nothing about it for 40ish years. Instead he sat in his cabin, alone in the woods, staring at the wall every damn night. All he did was wait for something to happen, until it never did. Don't be like Robert. How else could you possibly interpret the second half of his life?

Why does Lawrence of Arabia (1962) feel much more modern than Bridge on the River Kwai (1957)? I saw Bridge on the River Kwai for the first time last night, and loved it. But one thing that struck me is that despite being made only 5 years prior to Lawrence of Arabia, it feels a lot more old-fashioned. They're both excellent films, made by the same director, and they're both war films. But despite the similarities, with Lawrence I feel like I'm watching an early film from the modern era, but I didn't get that with Kwai at all. Was it the acting style, the cinematography, or something else? What makes a film feel modern to you?

Do you know where i can read the original articles and reviews that Godard, Truffaut and friends wrote for Cahiers Du Cinema before 1960? I have watched a bunch of Nouvelle Vague movies and read about the start of this movement which originated from these young people who were film critics for Cahiers Du Cinema magazine. What amazes me is that they were all very young and already had such deep knowledge about the art of cinema. I'm curious to read those early analyses before they started making movies on their own, and it would be great if you have recommendations for specific articles that are particularly revealing of how their ideas developed.

I decided to watch this movie for the first time, and I found it truly heartbreaking to witness the struggles of a couple trying to repair their marriage. It was emotional to see two people fighting to save their relationship while dealing with the problems that had driven them apart. I believe Dean has the potential to become a better man and a better husband. It's clear that he loves and cares for his daughter, Frankie, but his drinking habits are holding him back from becoming the person he could be. It's heartbreaking to see how his personal struggles and poor choices take a toll on his marriage and family, especially when there is still so much at stake. This is one of the reasons why I have always been against drinking and rarely drink alcohol myself. I believe excessive drinking can contribute to negative behaviour, poor decision-making, and domestic problems that can damage relationships and hurt the people we love. To me, a healthy relationship requires mutual respect, understanding, communication, and a willingness to take responsibility for our actions. Sometimes, saving a marriage means confronting our personal struggles before they destroy the very things that matter most in life.

Digger: What are professional critics smoking? Just posting to say that I liked the movie, so you might enjoy it too. I almost did not go to see it because of some bad reviews, namely on Roger Ebert where it was given 2/4. I did not like everything, I think the middle of the movie has a few forced scenes. But the beginning and the end did it for me. It has the merit of being inventive, with great universe creation, amazing actor performances, and a few great moments. It is like a very luxurious buffet: You might not like every exotic dish on the menu, but you surely will find a treat or two that you like. It would be a shame to not see that movie, because even if it misses a bit sometimes, it's still an interesting colossal endeavour.

Who saw The Exorcist (1973) in theaters? Curious to hear any personal accounts of what it was like to experience The Exorcist for the first time, including the lead-up to the actual release. I've always been fascinated by the lore that the original theatrical trailer made people physically ill (there is a ton of flashing), to the point Warner Bros. eventually pulled it. This film is still terrifying to me today, so I can't imagine how I would have reacted back then!

Begotten (1989) - Music Box Theatre w/ Elias Merhige. Just wanted to make a post; I saw Begotten for the first time at the music box with the director last night! It was amazing, they had restored it so the audio was pretty clean. However I think the thing that really stuck with me was the Q&A after. I've really struggled lately with how people talk about and consume film. It's more of context of what the film represents than being present and having an emotional engagement with it. Elias had this great line where he said something along the lines of, "film is a visual media but we're trying to use it to do mediocre literature". I think I wanted to hear other people's thoughts on the movie as of today? In the context of how something like it exists and more micro level stuff/ thoughts if you were at the Q&A

Movies or Shows that depict living life with PTSD. I really liked The Falcon and the Winter Soldier's depiction of Bucky's PTSD. It showed him genuinely trying to connect with people, get mental help, and work on himself, and how hard this is with PTSD. I want more shows or movies that aren't a super depressing self pity fest depicting life after trauma. I want to see the protagonist live life with their PTSD, not despite of it. Where the character works on themself and with the other people around them, and in the end has a happy ending where they have friends, community, and still get the help they need.

Thoughts on Brazil? I re-watched Brazil and I really loved the film. It is most definitely a Terry Gilliam film. Every scene in the film is just perfection and every scene is just so surreal and original. The acting is great as well. Jonathan Pryce was great as Sam Lowry and DeNiro honestly surprised me with his role as Harry Tuttle. Kim Greist was okay as Jill, but I was indifferent with her performance. I also know about the behind the scenes conflicts with the film, with Gilliam struggling to get the film released in the USA and Universal making a "Love Conquers All" Cut before shelving the film entirely. I haven't seen the Love Conquers All Cut and I wonder how different it is. I also think a good companion piece for Brazil is 1984 with John Hurt. What are your thoughts on Brazil? What do you think of the Love Conquers All Cut and how different is it from Gilliam's Cut?

After waiting a year for HOPE to come out, I finally saw it last night and loved it, then did my usual thing of checking out what other people are saying on Reddit and the like—and I am a bit appalled. This, as they say, is why we can't have nice things. People keep making ridiculous suggestions that the film is a parody of the action genre (it's not, though it is a subversion of it), or that the story is "all over the place" (pfft), etc. Nonsense. This is not one of those dumb action films somebody started without a script because such-and-such was only available through May. It's a smart movie, made by someone with a track record of making smart movies, and worth engaging with. So let's do a breakdown of what this film's about and some of the elements I enjoyed about it. As a note, I'm not Korean, but I spent a couple years in Korea, so I probably got more out of it than a lot of international viewers and a lot less than native ones. It is of course possible that I have misinterpreted some of its points. That said, I am a professionally published writer myself, albeit nobody important, meaning I at least know what themes and motifs are and I don't misuse the term "plot hole." I've also watched all of Na's stuff and a fair number of other Korean movies, so I recognize some Korean cinema tropes. THE STORY: INFILTRATION: When the movie opens, we find ourselves to be in a village close to the North Korean border. Signs everywhere warn residents to watch for infiltrators from the North and report anyone suspicious. If such signs were shown just once we might brush them aside as scene-setting, but they pop up multiple times, so we know they matter. This is a movie about our fear of others. THE HUNTERS: But who are the others? North Korean spies are the first others that get mentioned, but the first ones that we actually see are the hunters. One of the hunters mentions that it doesn't matter if the chief of police gets mad at him because he's getting "back on the boat" soon, which probably means he's one of the ethnic Koreans from Northeast China. Na Hong-Jin has made a movie about the plight of some of these people (THE YELLOW SEA, 2010); they come to South Korea by boat to work illegally. THE ALIENS: Of course, the star infiltrators of the movie are the aliens. The first alien is depicted as a vicious monster rampaging through town before we find out that it was just looking for its child and was murdered for its trouble. THE CONFLICT: The humanization of the aliens in this movie results in an unusual emotional conflict during the movie's action sequences. "HOPE": At the movie's end, we start getting translations of the aliens' dialogue, and a new plot seems to come out of nowhere regarding the death of the aliens' emperor and the need to find their prince. CONCLUSION: What we have here is a film about our fear of the other, particularly immigrants, and the awful things we do to them rather than understand them or reach out a helping hand. OK, that's the meaning I got. THE UNKILLABLE MAN: The hunter Ko Sung-ki appears to be immortal; every time he receives a blow that is likely to kill him, he gets up again. THE UNEXPECTED BAD-ASS: Officer Yim arrives on the scene in action-movie bad-ass mode, striking the first serious blow against an alien after it's devastated the town. THE SHERIFF: Hwang Jung-min plays Ko as a police chief who likes to throw his weight around a bit. At the end of the movie he says he "feels weird" (in the English subtitles). We should, too.

The Beyond (1981) feels less like Hell invading reality and more like reality slowly becoming Hell. What interests me most about The Beyond is how space gradually stops making sense. At first, the supernatural is tied to specific places: the hotel, the gateway, certain rooms. But by the end, John and Liza leave the hospital and somehow end up back at the hotel, then enter the wasteland where every direction leads nowhere. That makes me wonder if the film's apparent incoherence is partly deliberate. Maybe Hell isn't simply another place they enter. Maybe reality itself is losing causality, distance, and direction. Do you think that makes the film's loose narrative more effective, or is that reading too generous to Fulci?

anyone fond of Hal Hartley's works? I just saw his film "Meanwhile" which was my 9th film of his filmography and I gotta say he's spot on 9 for 9 thus far. It's actually incredible stuff, I've never encountered a more consistent filmography. Every single film has a stark script that's both sardonic, sincere at the same time. I'm curious why he didn't end up receiving the same fame as his other contemporary indie filmmakers like Jarmusch or Tarantino. His style is one of a kind.

Hi everyone! I'm working on a research project for my masters about the relationship between reading a book and watching its film adaptation, specifically focusing on how people imagine fictional spaces while reading and how those mental images compare with the spaces presented on screen. When a film adaptation comes along, it presents us with a concrete visual interpretation of those spaces. Sometimes the locations look almost exactly as we imagined them; other times, they look completely different. Does seeing a film's version of a place change how we remember or imagine it? Do we feel disappointed when a location doesn't match our mental image, or can the filmmaker's interpretation become even more convincing than our own? For this project, I'm particularly interested in The Lord of the Rings, since Tolkien's descriptions of Middle-earth have inspired readers to imagine its landscapes in their own ways, while Peter Jackson's film trilogy offers a highly recognizable visual interpretation of that world. I'm hoping to find at least 50 people who have both read The Lord of the Rings and watched its film adaptations and would be willing to participate in a short survey. If you've both read the books and watched the films please let me know in the comments! If you have any thoughts on this topic, I'd also love to hear them.

The end of inception is an insanely accurate representation of waking from a rough dream. Like, holy crap i felt the intensity every minute through. I still knew it was a big heist in a dream but as someone who has vivid dreams, cobb waking up on the plane in distress only to be met with the flight attendant "do you need immigration forms sir?" "Thank you" Its insanely accurate. The whole plot is based around this intense dream and after going through hell and back, lo and behold, you're awake. Back to normal. I know in-universe cobb got home to his kids and destroyed Fischer's empire, so it had HUGE repercussions. It wasnt really just a dream. But the whole concept of a dream was fleshed out unbelievably well in this movie. You know its bs, it fleshes the plot out so you forget its bs and take it seriously-- THEN BAM. You're woken up on a flight.

Is Taxi Driver overhyped? Just saw Taxi Driver (1976). I really liked how the film looks, but it felt bizarrely confusing. Only thing I could take away was, the protagonist is a self-flagellating contradictional man. He uses the existence of his perceived ideas of "scum of society" to vent out his frustrations. Like I get it, he's a lonely sociopath. Now what? What does the plot or story do with it? "We are lucky he took out his anger on evil people, and hence he was made a hero." I am maybe just conflicted on what all this praise is about, over such a mediocre story about a loner. I looked up online and saw paragraphs from people about it being a "social commentary," which is obvious. I thought that was the job of the movie? It just feels like a pointless vlog shot well in 1976.

Bitter Rice (1949) - an intensely filmed Neo-Realist drama deploying mixed Aesthetics. I've been on a Film Noir kick for a while, so I was a little surprised when watching the supposedly Noir-ish Italian Bitter Rice to only find a few stylistic nods in that direction. The film seems not Noir at all, so much as a rich Hollywood toned imagining of Neo-Realist embraced women. It's a spectacular film of energy, with big camera dynamics in beautiful, contrastive black and white. Not only is it female lead driven, but also throngs of female workers and vivid captures of work conditions, clashing together these two stylistic worlds. Some of the women singing scenes, and rain-drenched photography create whole auras of women's work and labor that are unexpectedly moving. It's about the attempted theft of the annual rice harvest in the Po Valley, in the aftermath of World War 2. Criticized for not being Neo-Realist enough, and employing Hollywood glamour styling and some Noir pulp, actually makes the film more interesting.
